# Third-party assets

Everything the app ships that someone else made, with where it came from and the
licence it carries: the bundled `.woff2` faces under `web/assets/fonts/`, one
sprite of drawings, and the code under `Code` below. Each licence text sits
beside the thing it covers in the repository, which is what redistributing the
source requires — condition 2 of the OFL, and the notice condition of the MIT
and Apache licences.

The drawings and the sounds are in `SHELL` (`web/sw.js`), so an installed app
that shows them and makes them offline carries their notices with them. The font
licences are not, which is a gap rather than a decision: the faces predate that
reading and moving them into the shell is a change worth making on its own.
Neither are the vendored decoders, and that one *is* a decision — they are
loaded only when a file that needs them is imported, and precaching megabytes
for a format most boards never hold is the trade their own module headers argue
against.

Code rather than an asset changes nothing about the terms, and it is worth
saying why. MIT, Apache-2.0 and Zlib into GPL-3.0-or-later are all compatible in
that direction — the combined work goes out under the GPL — but the notice
condition travels with the source, so the copyright line stays at the top of
every vendored file, the licence text ships beside it, and none of it can be
tidied away as boilerplate.

## Drawings

| Set | File | Source | Licence | Licence file |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Phosphor Icons | `web/assets/stickers.svg` | https://github.com/phosphor-icons/core | MIT | `web/assets/phosphor-LICENSE.txt` |
| Simple Icons | `web/assets/js/canvas/brands.ts` | https://github.com/simple-icons/simple-icons | CC0-1.0 | — (public domain, no notice required) |

The sticker sprite is forty-five Phosphor glyphs, vendored at the revision
pinned in `tools/gen-stickers.mjs` and regenerated by it. Two weights are used —
`duotone` for shapes with a body and `bold` for the marks that are a line — and
the only change made to any outline is to the *paint*: Phosphor's own files put
`fill="currentColor"` on the root and mark the duotone background layer with
`opacity="0.2"`, and the generator inverts that so the background inherits
mbrd's paper and the foreground takes the tint. No path data is touched.

`web/assets/icons.svg`, the app's own chrome sprite, is drawn here and is not
third-party. The two are separate files for the reason the head of each states.

The brand marks in `canvas/brands.ts` are the logos of the sites a link card can
point at, drawn in the offer chip so a plain link reads like the player cards
rather than fetching a favicon per domain. Path data only, one path per brand on
Simple Icons' own `0 0 24 24` grid, unmodified. Simple Icons releases the paths
under CC0, which waives the notice — the licence column records provenance, not
an obligation. The logos themselves are the trademarks of their owners; CC0
covers the path data, not any right in the mark. Each is drawn in its brand
colour where that reads on the board paper, and in the board ink where the mark
is black (X, GitHub, Patreon, TikTok, Threads, Medium).

## Music

| Track | File | Source | Licence | Licence file |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ambient Piano, by leberch | `web/assets/audio/clean-loop.opus` | https://pixabay.com/music/ambient-ambient-piano-595681/ | Pixabay Content License | — (no notice required) |

The loop the cleaning mode plays. The Pixabay Content License grants irrevocable
use with no attribution asked for, so the row above and the line in the credits
sheet record where it came from rather than discharging a condition. It is the
only recorded audio the app carries — everything else you hear is synthesised by
Cuelume from numbers — and it is deliberately outside `SHELL` (`web/sw.js`), so
nobody pays a megabyte of precache for a mode most people never open.

Ten vendored builds, none of them modified, each loaded only when a file or a
command that needs it is used and none of them in `SHELL`.

**onnxruntime-web** runs **u2netp**, the model behind the background remover,
in a worker (`web/assets/js/canvas/matte-worker.js`). `canvas/matte.ts` pins
both, and `tests/matte-vendor.test.js` holds the pin to the files. The obvious
larger models are CC BY-NC or AGPL and cannot ship here; u2netp is Apache-2.0.

**pdf.js** renders page one of a PDF — and of an `.ai`, which is a PDF — to a
raster the card draws. It is carried rather than fetched for a reason worth
keeping written down: `script-src 'self'` refused the CDN copy outright on the
deployed site while working perfectly on the dev server, so the feature was dead
exactly where anybody else would see it. `web/assets/js/import/pdf.ts` argues it
at length and pins the version, and `tests/pdf-vendor.test.js` holds the pin to
the bytes actually in the directory.

**UTIF.js** decodes a TIFF, which is the one ordinary picture format no engine
but Safari draws and the one with nothing else to fall back on: a scan carries
no embedded JPEG for the RAW reader to find and no thumbnail for the document
reader to look up. **pako** is its inflate, and only its inflate — TIFF's ZIP
compression, which Photoshop writes by default. Both run inside
`web/assets/js/import/tiff-worker.js`, off the main thread, because the decode
is straight-line JavaScript over every pixel of what may be a 400-megapixel
scan. Neither touches the DOM and neither reaches any host.

**libarchive.js** opens the archives the hand-written readers do not: 7z, RAR,
and a ZIP that uses ZIP64 or a method other than deflate
(`web/assets/js/import/archive.ts`). It is a wrapper round
[libarchive](https://github.com/libarchive/libarchive), compiled to
WebAssembly and distributed under libarchive's own two-clause BSD licence
(https://github.com/libarchive/libarchive/blob/master/COPYING). The wasm runs
in a module worker with the policy dropped (`web/_headers`), is loaded on the
first archive that needs it, and reads the one file it is handed. Its flat
entry list is used rather than its tree, since the tree is built by assigning
path segments as object keys.

**occt-import-js** is Open CASCADE Technology (https://dev.opencascade.org)
compiled to WebAssembly, and it is the only entry here whose licence changes how
it may be loaded. STEP and IGES contain no triangles - they describe a solid as
trimmed surfaces and the topology between them - so drawing one means running a
geometry kernel. `web/assets/js/mesh/occt-worker.js` runs this one, off the main
thread and with the site's Content-Security-Policy removed for that file alone;
`web/assets/js/mesh/occt.ts` pins the version and `tests/occt-vendor.test.js`
holds the pin to the bytes in the directory.

Both the wrapper and the kernel are LGPL-2.1. This project is GPL-3.0-or-later,
and the two are not compatible as one work - so they are not one work. The
kernel is carried as a standalone pair of files, loaded at run time by a worker
and never passed through esbuild, which is LGPL-2.1 section 6: a work that
*uses* the library, relinkable against another build of it without rebuilding
anything here, may carry terms of its own. Bundling `occt-import-js.js` into
`web/assets/app.js` would end that and is the one thing not to do with it.

The app can also do without this one. `mesh/step.ts` and
`mesh/iges.ts` read both formats without it, and are what happens when the
kernel does not load - see the head of `mesh/occt.ts`.

**libraw-wasm** is LibRaw 0.22.1 (https://www.libraw.org) compiled to
WebAssembly with Little CMS 2.19.1 and Emscripten's libjpeg and zlib ports. It
develops a camera RAW: the Demosaic row on a RAW card, and Optimize, which
develops a RAW before it shrinks it like any photograph.
`web/assets/js/optimize/demosaic.ts` pins the version and
`tests/libraw-vendor.test.js` holds the pin to the files. The wrapper is ISC.
LibRaw is offered under LGPL-2.1 or CDDL-1.0 and is taken here under LGPL-2.1,
on the argument made for OCCT above: the four files are loaded at run time by a
module worker the wrapper spawns, with the site policy removed for that file
alone (`web/_headers`), and none of them passes through esbuild. Replacing
`libraw.wasm` with another build of it needs nothing here rebuilt. Without it a
RAW card keeps the preview its camera stored in the file (`import/preview.ts`),
which is what every RAW card drew before this arrived.

**heic2any** is libheif and libde265 compiled to *JavaScript* rather than
WebAssembly — which is why it is a megabyte and a third, and why it is the
second of two HEIC decoders rather than the first. `import/heif.ts` reads the
container itself and gives the HEVC to WebCodecs, which is the machine's own
decoder and needs no download; this is what runs when `VideoDecoder` is absent,
which it is on every origin that is not secure. That file pins the version, and
the same run-time-loading argument made for OCCT and LibRaw above applies
unchanged: `web/assets/js/import/heif-worker.js` loads it with
`importScripts`, the site policy is removed for that worker alone
(`web/_headers`), and nothing here passes through esbuild. The exemption is for
`new Function` rather than for wasm — Emscripten's embind builds libheif's
exports with it, and the page carries no `'unsafe-eval'`. The wrapper is MIT;
libheif and libde265 are LGPL-3.0-or-later, by the same authors, and are taken
here under that.

The ffmpeg core (`@ffmpeg/core` 0.12.6, MIT over LGPL-2.1 — the npm package is
MIT and the FFmpeg build inside it is LGPL-2.1 —
https://github.com/ffmpegwasm/ffmpeg.wasm) is deliberately *not* in the table
above: it ships with nothing, is not in this repository, and is fetched from
jsdelivr on first use — see `web/assets/js/optimize/media.ts`, which is the one
place in the app that reaches a host for code, and `web/_headers`, which permits
that one host and nothing else. It is listed here because a reader of this file
wants to know what runs, not only what is committed.

**The desktop build ships FFmpeg itself, and that one is GPL-3.0.** Not the same
thing as the paragraph above and not on the same terms: `@ffmpeg/core` is an
LGPL build fetched by a browser at run time, and this is a GPL static executable
inside a download. It is FFmpeg (https://github.com/FFmpeg/FFmpeg), 7.1 on Windows and macOS and
7.0.2 on Linux, one prebuilt binary per platform, pinned by version in
`desktop/scripts/fetch-ffmpeg.mjs` — GyanD's `essentials` build on Windows
(https://github.com/GyanD/codexffmpeg), evermeet.cx's on macOS
(https://evermeet.cx/ffmpeg/), John Van Sickle's static build on Linux
(https://johnvansickle.com/ffmpeg/). **Every one of them is a GPL build with no
non-free codec in it**, which is the condition that matters: `libfdk-aac` or
`libnpp` in any of the three would make the whole download undistributable under
any licence, whatever the builder's own page says. The head of
`fetch-ffmpeg.mjs` argues that at length and is where a fourth platform would be
added.

GPL-3.0 into GPL-3.0-or-later is the one direction that needs no argument, but
it carries more than a notice: conveying the binary means offering its source.
The pinned release page each URL above points into publishes the exact source
tarball beside the build, which is the offer §6(d)'s "access to copy from a
designated place" describes, and naming the three of them here is what makes
that offer findable. The binary is fetched at release time rather than committed
— 80-odd megabytes per platform, `desktop/resources/ffmpeg/` is gitignored — so
a checkout carries none of it and a developer who never runs the script gets a
desktop that falls through to the wasm path above.

Dependencies of the `desktop/` and `mobile/` packages rather than vendored
files, so their licence texts ship inside each installer's `node_modules` or
APK, where electron-builder and Gradle put them. libvips is carried by sharp as
a separate shared library, which is the relinkable form LGPL-3.0 asks for.

## Cuelume

The interface sounds. Seventeen recipes — each a handful of numbers rather than
an audio file — and the Web Audio graph that renders them, taken as source and
forked rather than depended on, since the app has no runtime dependencies and
this is about two hundred lines.

Two thirds of upstream is here and the missing third is deliberate: `bind.ts`
and `index.ts` are not vendored. `bind()` installs four capture-phase listeners
on `document` and reads `data-cuelume-*` attributes off whatever the event
landed on, which for a library is exactly right and here is a second event
listener beside `cmds`, a second markup contract beside `data-cmd`, and a hover
tick on a canvas somebody sweeps a pointer across without meaning anything by
it. The head of `engine.ts` argues all three at length.

What was changed from upstream is listed at the top of each file. In summary:
the cue map and the whimsy tiers, which have no counterpart there; a repeat
guard and a detune; the context suspending after a spell of quiet; the ambient
audio session; and the level being read from `prefs.ts` rather than set by the
host. No recipe number was altered.

Every face here is subset to Latin and Latin Extended rather than shipped whole,
and that is the only change made to any of them: all variation axes are intact,
including Playfair's `wdth`, which was briefly instanced out to save 312KB and
has been restored. Subsetting for a delivery format is what the OFL FAQ covers
under subsetting, and is how Google Fonts itself serves these families under
their own names. No outline was redrawn and no Reserved Font Name is used for
anything the original authors did not draw.
